summary: On August 15, 2133, Bob coordinates ROAMers assembling ship components while Dr. Doucette covers for Dr. Landers. Their conversation recounts Old Handeltown's origins in Salem, Oregon, the city's renaming and memorial, the memorial's nuclear destruction, and the later move of Handeltown to Portland, as well as the State's expectation of public piety. Bob learns that Piety Monitors may be among security patrols and that the Ministry of Proper Thought is a feared consequence of confronting them. When he asks how his handlers will ensure he follows the mission after release, Doucette says his software contains undisclosed safeguards; Bob worries that they may compel choices while still feeling like his own.

introducing.name: Dr. Doucette
introducing.current_state: Covering for Dr. Landers while Bob continues his training and assembly work.

introducing.name: translation routine
introducing.description: A routine that interprets the standard twenty-second-century accent so smoothly that differing speech patterns become effectively transparent to its user.

introducing.name: Old Handeltown
introducing.description: A historic Oregon city identified as Salem, Oregon and as Handel's birthplace. After Handel's death, the city changed its name and a large memorial was established in his honor. An unidentified person later destroyed the memorial with a pocket nuclear weapon after objecting. It was the only nuclear weapon deployed in North America, and advanced radiation treatment limited the resulting deaths.

updates.current_state: Continuing training and assembly as the sole remaining probe candidate. His software safeguards remain incompletely understood.
Away from the project while Dr. Doucette covers for him.

updates.description: Remote observation and manipulation devices directed through GUPPI. They come in varied sizes, can coordinate across scales, and need minimal supervision once their tasks, dependencies, and interruption conditions are defined. Without active intervention, they can work up to ten times faster. They can travel along floors, walls, and ceilings, carry video cameras for remote observation, and pick up vibrations transmitted through a wall when pressed against it. Reusable scripts automate many routine activities, leaving assembly work largely self-directed.
